doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Starting record reviews and the anti-jazz critics
summary: Baraka introduced him to Dan Morgenstern; critics attacked Coltrane, so he trusted his own ears.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: The poetry, did it lead somehow to writing record reviews and, or were your record reviews a way to make some income?

Yeah definitely. Let me see, Baraka got me into writing record reviews. He was doing it. And when I moved to New York he was my closest friend and he thought I could do it well and he introduced me to Dan Morgenstern who was the editor of not Down— Metronome magazine at the time, and Dan let me write some — I wrote introducing Archie Schepp article and he gave me some records to review, and so that’s how I got started in it. I wasn’t feeling all that qualified to do it to tell you the truth, but then when basically the jazz establishment, response to the new music convinced me that I ought to © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

do it because all these articles were coming out about anti-jazz and John Coltrane was considered to be anti-jazz as was Cecil and numerous others, Ornette and others. And so I would go to this concert, and I would go to this one at the Village Gate say, and I’d hear John Coltrane, he’d be wailing. And I’d leave there really feeling like I just had the soul rinsing that I had mentioned in those liner notes that you referred to, and just practically limp from the experience, and I’d open the magazine and see that John Coltrane was the worst thing that ever happened to jazz. You know. So I’m saying, “Okay A.B., either you can’t hear or they can’t hear.” You know? So that’s what gave me some confidence to write about it since it was being written about, the new music certainly being written about from a wrong-minded perspective and people were not open to it and could not hear what I heard. And I knew I had to trust my own experience most of all.
